summary: Two strands for ages 9–11: (1) the human LIFE COURSE — naming and ordering stages from birth to old age (baby, toddler, child, adolescent/puberty, young adult, middle-aged adult, elderly) and describing physical changes, with the key quantitative point that growth is UNEVEN (rapid in infancy, a spurt at puberty, then levelling off, not a steady slope); and (2) PUBERTY — the physical changes of adolescence (growth spurts, body-shape changes, development of adult features) and the core new mechanism that these are TRIGGERED BY HORMONES: chemical messengers released by glands, carried in the blood, that switch on changes elsewhere in the body. Teach puberty factually, calmly and inclusively, normalising that timing and rate vary widely between individuals and that some changes differ between sexes. Keep hormone detail conceptual (messengers that trigger change); leave named-hormone feedback loops for a later homeostasis topic.
misconceptions: 'People grow at a steady rate throughout childhood' — missing the uneven pattern and the pubertal growth spurt.
'Everyone goes through puberty at the same age' — missing the wide, normal variation in timing and rate.
'Hormones are something bad / only about mood' — rather than chemical messengers that coordinate normal body changes.
'Puberty happens suddenly / all at once' — it's a gradual process over several years.
'Growing up means only getting taller' — missing the range of body-shape and developmental changes.
'Adults keep growing taller' — height growth stops after puberty; other changes continue with age.

activities.title: Scrub the life timeline and uncover the uneven growth curve
steps: Move through the life stages in order from baby to elderly and label each one (baby, toddler, child, adolescent/puberty, young adult, middle-aged adult, elderly).

As you pass through each stage, watch a growth curve build up and describe the SHAPE of the line in your own words — where it is steep, where it becomes less steep (a slower, steadier rise in childhood), where it rises sharply again, and where it finally flattens.
Mark where growth is fastest (infancy), where it slows, where it surges again (puberty), and where height growth stops but other changes continue.

Look at a 'variation band' around the puberty stage that shows the same surge arriving at different ages for different people, and say in a sentence why two people the same age might be at different points.
activities.insight: Growth is not a steady, even slope: it comes in bursts — fast in infancy, slowing to a steadier rate in childhood, then a spurt at puberty before height growth stops — and the timing of the pubertal surge differs between people, within a wide range that is normal.

activities.title: Trace a hormone messenger from gland to change
steps: Release a messenger from a gland and follow its path as it travels in the blood to another part of the body.
Match the arriving messenger to the specific pubertal change it switches on, and state the cause-and-effect in one sentence: 'a chemical released here causes a change there'.
Explain, in your own words, how a signal made in one place can cause a change somewhere else via the blood.

Consider how the same kind of trigger — hormones — can switch on some different changes in different people, including some changes that differ between boys and girls, and explain that this happens partly because different glands in different bodies release somewhat different messengers, and bodies respond in different ways.
activities.insight: Hormones are chemical messengers released by glands and carried in the blood; a chemical released in one place triggers changes elsewhere in the body. The same kind of trigger (hormones) can switch on different changes in different individuals — including some that differ between sexes, partly because different glands release somewhat different messengers. This signal→change idea is the core new concept beyond simply naming stages.

activities.title: Ask the trusted expert the questions you'd rather not ask aloud
steps: Pose puberty questions to a friendly, factual school-nurse/health-educator persona (for example, 'is it normal to start at a different age from my friends?').
Read the factual, reassuring answer and restate the key fact it gives — especially that changes are normal and that timing and rate differ between people.
Identify any myth the answer corrects (for example, that puberty happens all at once) and say the accurate version.
activities.insight: Puberty questions have calm, factual answers; the kinds of changes are broadly shared (with some differing between sexes) but individual in timing and rate, and variation across a wide range is normal rather than a sign something is wrong.

activities.title: Explain why two identically-fed friends can differ
steps: Consider two 11-year-old friends who eat the same food and do the same exercise, but one has started puberty and the other hasn't.
Explain what is actually triggering the body changes and where that trigger comes from.

Say why eating more food or wanting it sooner does not itself start puberty, distinguishing the raw materials food supplies from the hormone signal that starts the changes (overall nutrition and health can shift timing somewhat, but the hormone signal is what starts the changes).
activities.insight: Puberty is triggered by hormones released by glands into the blood — not directly by diet, exercise, effort, or simply the passing of time (though overall nutrition and health can influence timing somewhat) — and because hormone timing differs between people, onset age varies.

checkQuestion: Two 11-year-old friends eat the same food and do the same exercise, but one has started puberty and the other hasn't. If puberty isn't simply caused by what you eat or how much you move, what is actually triggering these body changes — and where does that trigger come from?
checkAnswer: Puberty is triggered by hormones — chemical messengers released by glands into the blood — not directly by food or exercise. The hormones travel around the body and cause the physical changes, and because hormone timing differs between people, puberty starts at different ages for different individuals.
